abstract: Circulating cell-free DNA (cirDNA) fragmentation reflects chromatin organization and represents a promising source of cancer biomarkers. Here, we characterized the fragmentation patterns and nucleosome occupancy of Y chromosome (chrY) cirDNA in healthy individuals and cancer patients. In healthy males, we found that the shorter chrY-derived cirDNA fragments predominantly originate from heterochromatic regions. We also observed substantially lower nucleosome occupancy on chrY than on all other chromosomes, a finding independently supported by micrococcal nuclease digestion data. Remarkably, in patients with colorectal, pancreatic, lung and prostate cancer, the chrY-specific enrichment of shorter fragments was markedly attenuated, contrasting with the increased fragmentation usually observed in cancer when chromosome specificity is disregarded. We reproduced these observations in an independent local cohort of healthy and colorectal cancer patients. We could exploit ratios of short (100-147 bp) to long (147-200 bp) fragments between chrY and other chromosomes to discriminate healthy males from patients with colorectal, pancreatic, and lung cancers with AUCs above 0.98. Autosomes 19, 17, and 22 also displayed atypical fragment patterns, different from chrY and associated with gene density. This last observation was confirmed in females.
